title: Vib-Ribbon
subtitle: A rabbit on a line of music

body: Vib-Ribbon is NanaOn-Sha's PlayStation rhythm game, released in Japan on 9 December 1999. Vibri walks along a thin white line as music turns the route into obstacles. The drawing is deliberately spare: a rabbit, a moving path and enough shape to show the next action. Masaya Matsuura led the project after plans for a car advertisement changed into a standalone game. Rather than fill the screen with scenery, it makes the movement of a line carry both the landscape and the rhythm the player needs to follow.

Blocks, loops, waves and pits correspond to four different button inputs. Pressing at the right moment lets Vibri cross each shape; combined obstacles require both responses together. Repeated mistakes transform the rabbit into a frog and then an insect, while successful play can restore her or produce the higher-scoring Super Vibri form. Damage is therefore visible in the character rather than only in a separate meter. The route remains simple to describe, but reading joined shapes and responding to the music gives the small vocabulary room to become demanding.

The software loads into the PlayStation's memory, allowing the game disc to be removed and replaced with an audio CD. Vib-Ribbon then generates routes from that record's tracks. Six built-in songs provide the initial courses, with music credited to Laugh and Peace and Matsuura, but a personal collection can supply further journeys. The idea changes an ordinary household object into level material. Europe received the original in 2000; North America first received the game through PlayStation Network in 2014, extending the life of a project whose strongest feature was its openness to other music.
